tweet.text:
THE PENTAGON IS STARTING TO PUT QUANTUM IN EVERYTHING. 

HERE’S THE LIST.

This week the Department of War put $350M into quantum and said they needed weapons that are “more lethal, cost-effective and manufacturable.”

Total Quantum funding commitments this year has already reached $3.4 billion. HERE’s what it’s already going into.

Submarines: Quantum magnetometers detect the tiny magnetic field a steel hull leaves in the ocean. Degaussing doesn’t fully remove it. The 70 year advantage of hiding underwater is ending.

Aircraft: The Air Force flew a jet for 4 hours over the Pacific with GPS off, navigating by Earth’s magnetic field with a quantum sensor. Jamming GPS doesn’t work on a plane that isn’t using it.

Ships: A vessel crossed the Coral Sea with no GPS, navigating by gravity. Quantum gravimeters read the seafloor’s pull and match it to a map.

Drones: The Pentagon is putting quantum navigation on cheap disposable drones. A $20,000 drone that can’t be jammed changes the math on every air defense system.

Helicopters: DARPA strapped quantum sensors to a helicopter to see if they survive vibration and they did.

Radios: One Rydberg atom antenna receives the entire radio spectrum at once. Most antenna's in the world are tuned to one band. This one hears all of them.

Soldiers: The Army wants helmets that read brain activity in the field. Quantum magnetometers are the only sensors small enough to do it without a shielded room.

Nuclear weapons: The Pentagon says quantum threatens the system that controls them, and NIST is putting quantum sensors on nuclear material detection.

Then the layer on top: Lockheed built a dedicated quantum weapons center, NATO put quantum on a military schedule, and DARPA just picked IBM, IonQ, Atom Computing and Diraq to build the computer that designs the next generation and so much more. 

$INFQ $IONQ $QBTS $QNT

quote.text:
THE MILITARY IS GOING QUANTUM. 

THESE 7 COMPANIES ARE IN POSITION TO WIN.

Farseer is DIU's $200 million program to put quantum sensors into the military within months with magnetometers, gravity gradiometers, tactical clocks, and components. Proposals closed in July. Winners haven't been named. Here's who I think gets picked, and why.

$HON: A jet running Honeywell's quantum navigation system flew four hours over the Pacific with GPS switched off, reading Earth's magnetic field to stay on course, 89% more accurate than standard backups. It was a test for this same Pentagon office, grown out of Farseer's predecessor program, and a C-17 is next. 

@qctrlHQ: Its quantum gravimeter just navigated a ship across the Coral Sea with no GPS and no stabilization. Gravity gradiometers are a named Farseer lane, and it has DIU and DARPA history.

$INFQ: Its Tiqker clocks are in Navy programs, its Rydberg RF receivers are with the Army, and it's building NASA's quantum gravity gradiometer, which covers three of Farseer's four lanes. On June 22nd, the day before Farseer launched, its CEO was in the Oval Office for the quantum executive orders, the only quantum sensing company in the room alongside IBM and Google.

$IONQ: through their Vector Atomic acquisition, their portable atomic clocks won under the last DIU program. IonQ owns it now, and tactical clocks are a Farseer lane.

$LMT: Launched its quantum center last week and was a previous DIU awardee. Most likely as the integrator putting sensors on platforms.

@SandboxAQ: AQNav has flown quantum magnetic navigation on Air Force aircraft. Not on the last DIU list, but the most operational magnetic navigation system out there.

AOSense: Atom-interferometry gravimeters and inertial sensors, decades of defense work, previous DIU awardee.

Time will tell soon enough who gets in, bookmark this!

$INFQ $IONQ $LMT
